title: Im Leslie Knope

jokes.text: Absotootly, I am. Very sorry that I just used that word.
jokes.setup: Serious political recruiters ask Leslie if she's interested in running for office — a formal, high-stakes moment.
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds with the goofy made-up word 'Absotootly' and immediately, earnestly apologizes for it.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie Knope character comedy — she is so eager and well-meaning that she blurts out a childish word in a professional moment, then immediately self-corrects with earnest sincerity. The self-awareness ('Very sorry') makes it land harder than pure obliviousness would. High character integration because only Leslie would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm ready to serve the people of Pawnee with integrity and professionalism.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Together, we can build a more... prosperous... and munificent future!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, did I just say munificent? I meant magnificent. Or... munificent is a word, right? Either way, I'm sorry.

jokes.text: Leslie's long pause before answering 'Nope' to whether there's a scandal — she is secretly dating her boss Ben.
jokes.setup: The political recruiters ask if there's any scandal in her life they should know about.
jokes.punchline: A beat of silence followed by a flat 'Nope' — while the audience knows she is actively hiding a relationship with her boss.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely structural — the audience is ahead of the recruiters. The pause and the breezy 'Nope' are perfectly timed irony. The rewatch bonus is high because on second viewing the hypocrisy is even richer. Economy is near-perfect: one word does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have nothing to hide. My entire life is an open book. There are no secrets, no scandals, nothing embarrassing in my past whatsoever.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we just found photos of you and—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, well, there's that one thing.

jokes.text: "Uh-oh! Do you want to go back to saying 'yay'?" / "Yes, please. Yay! Yay!"
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are celebrating Leslie's potential candidacy, then Ann raises the problem of Leslie's secret relationship with Ben.
jokes.punchline: Ann offers to retreat back to pure celebration, and Leslie eagerly agrees, both shouting 'Yay!' to avoid the problem.
jokes.explanation: A warm, character-driven laugh that also efficiently sets up the episode's central conflict. The 'going back to yay' bit is a charming bit of emotional avoidance that is very true to both characters. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is it! This is my moment! I'm running for City Council and I'm going to win!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's amazing! We're so excited for you!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, right? I've been preparing for this my whole—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben. I can't be with Ben. The ethics violations. He's the Deputy Director.

jokes.text: "My ex-wife, Tammy, is back." / "No, my other ex-wife, Tammy. Tammy One."
jokes.setup: Ron is in a panic and tells Leslie his ex-wife Tammy is back.
jokes.punchline: Leslie assumes it's the Tammy the audience knows; Ron clarifies it's a DIFFERENT ex-wife, also named Tammy — 'Tammy One.'
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The reveal that Ron has TWO ex-wives named Tammy is an absurdist escalation that also feels completely plausible for Ron Swanson's character. The structure is clean (setup, misdirection, correction) and the joke pays off on multiple levels — it's funny immediately and funnier the more you think about what it says about Ron's romantic history. High character integration: only Ron Swanson could have two ex-wives named Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You know what? I could go back to not knowing any of this stuff. Ignorance is bliss.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes. Please do that.

jokes.text: Ron announces he is using all 228 accumulated personal days starting immediately and puts Leslie in charge.
jokes.setup: Ron is terrified of Tammy One and needs to escape the office.
jokes.punchline: He has somehow accumulated 228 personal days — implying he has never once used a personal day — and deploys them all at once as a getaway.
jokes.explanation: 228 days is a specific, funny number that implies Ron has never taken a day off in his life — consistent with his work ethic and stoicism. Using all of them simultaneously to flee from his ex-wife is perfectly Ron. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have been married twice. Both times to a woman named Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy Two was the worst thing that ever happened to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But Tammy One... Tammy One tried to sabotage the entire Parks Department. So it's a tough call.

jokes.text: "Also, I keep a sizable supply of ground chuck in my desk. Remove it or it will begin to smell. Godspeed."
jokes.setup: Ron is dramatically fleeing the office, giving Leslie last-minute instructions.
jokes.punchline: As a final, completely serious directive, he warns her about the raw meat he stores in his desk drawer.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron storing raw ground beef in his desk is perfectly on-brand, delivered with complete deadpan seriousness as though it is a totally normal professional matter. The word 'sizable' and the capper 'Godspeed' elevate this beyond a simple character quirk into a beautifully written comedic moment. The economy is excellent — three short sentences, maximum laugh. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have accumulated 3,400 hours of unused vacation days. I'm taking them all at once. My ex-wife Tammy will never find me.

jokes.text: Godspeed. / Hey, Ron. Move. / Oh, jeez. [Ron physically scrambling away from Tammy One's approach]
jokes.setup: Ron says 'Godspeed' dramatically and departs — then is immediately intercepted or has to scramble
jokes.punchline: The dramatic exit is undercut by Ron having to physically hurry/dodge — 'Oh, jeez' as Ron's barely suppressed panic
jokes.explanation: The visual of the stoic Ron Swanson scrambling and saying 'Oh, jeez' is inherently funny — physical comedy from someone who never shows fear. The rewatch bonus is high because on subsequent viewings the audience knows the terror of Tammy One.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm keeping some raw meat in my desk drawer. It's for emergencies.

jokes.text: "Warning. High levels of swagger coming through. Tommy Haverford back at the Parks Department. Entertainment 720 hockey jersey, anybody? Branded mouse pad?"
jokes.setup: Tom returns to the Parks Department having left to start his entertainment company.
jokes.punchline: His grand re-entrance involves announcing his own swagger and offering branded merchandise — including a mouse pad — as though these are impressive status symbols.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford character comedy. The specific pairing of 'hockey jersey' and 'branded mouse pad' as evidence of his empire is funny because of the absurd gap between his self-image and reality. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, wait! Where are you going?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: Ronald.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no.

jokes.text: "Donna, you look amazing. How are the kids?" / "I don't have kids." / "Wow. How long has it been?" / "Three weeks."
jokes.setup: Tom greets Donna with over-the-top familiarity as though returning from a long journey.
jokes.punchline: It has been three weeks. He doesn't even know if she has kids.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured mini-joke. Tom's performative grandeur ('you look amazing, how are the kids') is punctured by Donna's flat 'I don't have kids' — and then the final reveal that only three weeks have passed makes it a perfect escalating triple. The structure is textbook and the economy is excellent. One of the tighter setups of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hello, everybody. It is I, Tom Haverford, entrepreneur, visionary, and small business owner. I have returned.

jokes.text: Entertainment 720 hockey jersey, anybody? Branded mouse pad? Entertainment 720 is just a little multinational entertainment company that I started with my boy Jean-Ralphio.
jokes.setup: Tom is distributing branded merchandise for his new company
jokes.punchline: 'A little multinational entertainment company' — the casual undersell of 'little' paired with 'multinational' is absurdly grandiose, plus 'my boy Jean-Ralphio' grounds it in the show's universe
jokes.explanation: The self-contradiction of 'little multinational' is funny. Jean-Ralphio's name is inherently funny. The merchandise distribution at a government office has absurdist charm.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I can't actually explain what my business does.

jokes.text: Leslie's confession that while other girls played with Barbies, she played with a Geraldine Ferraro action figure she made herself by gluing a photo onto a Popsicle stick.
jokes.setup: Leslie is expressing her lifelong passion for public office.
jokes.punchline: Her childhood version of playing with dolls was a homemade Geraldine Ferraro Popsicle stick figure — the specificity of both the politician chosen and the DIY method is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's best jokes. The specificity of Geraldine Ferraro (not a generic politician — the first female VP candidate), combined with the pathos and comedy of a little girl gluing a photo to a Popsicle stick because no such toy existed, is both deeply funny and deeply character-revealing. It's also touching, which elevates it. Only Leslie Knope has this backstory. High originality, exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh man, it feels like I've been gone for years! So much has changed!

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Tom, you were only gone three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, who are you again?

jokes.text: "Oh, Ann. You beautiful, naive, sophisticated newborn baby."
jokes.setup: Ann asks why Leslie can't just keep sneaking around with Ben instead of breaking up.
jokes.punchline: Leslie addresses Ann with a string of contradictory, endearing adjectives that simultaneously compliment and dismiss her.
jokes.explanation: The single most quotable line of the episode and one of Parks and Recreation's most beloved recurring joke structures — Leslie's elaborate, contradictory compliments to Ann. 'Beautiful, naive, sophisticated newborn baby' is a masterpiece of internal contradiction that somehow feels warm and condescending at once. It became a cultural reference point for the show. High originality (the contradictory compliment structure is distinctive), near-perfect economy, and the highest character integration possible — this joke could ONLY be Leslie talking to Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what do you think of my position papers?

dialogue.speaker: Political advisor
dialogue.line: Leslie, these are great, but you're running for City Council in Pawnee, Indiana. You have forty pages on Middle East peace accords.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I like to be thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Political advisor
dialogue.line: You also wrote a comprehensive trade policy with the European Union. Pawnee doesn't have trade relations with the European Union.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: "I have a plan, and it's really good. I'm going to postpone telling him until you figure out what I'm supposed to do. So, get cracking. / How is this on me?"
jokes.setup: Leslie says she has a really good plan for dealing with the Ben situation.
jokes.punchline: The 'plan' is to push all responsibility onto Ann and procrastinate.
jokes.explanation: A functional joke about Leslie's denial and her tendency to assign problems to others while maintaining confidence. Ann's 'How is this on me?' is a good straight-man reaction. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When I was a little girl, I made an action figure out of a Barbie doll and some pipe cleaners. I named her Senator Barbara and she fought crime and passed legislation.

jokes.text: God, who keeps emailing me? A penis.
jokes.setup: Leslie is frustrated by constant notifications on her phone during a serious conversation
jokes.punchline: The mundane 'who keeps emailing me' is answered with 'A penis' — the reveal of the Jerry sexting scandal
jokes.explanation: The misdirection of 'who keeps emailing me' followed immediately by 'A penis' is a perfectly timed reveal. The economy is excellent — one word delivers the punchline. Strong structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Who were you meeting with?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, just my... my dentist. Dr. Teeth McFloss. He's very exclusive. Only takes patients on Tuesdays and Saturdays, but also Wednesdays. He's very flexible with his schedule. We were discussing my gums, which are — I'm very proud of them.

jokes.text: A penis photo is being emailed to every woman in the government — including Leslie's phone — and Andy's reaction is "Respect. That's a baller move. Pun intended."
jokes.setup: A government employee has accidentally (or intentionally) sent a lewd photo to every woman in city government.
jokes.punchline: Andy responds with genuine admiration for the boldness of the act, and then congratulates himself on the pun 'baller.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's sincere admiration for a lewd act is perfectly in character, and his proud awareness of his own pun is a great secondary beat. 'Pun intended' after 'baller' is a solid wordplay moment. High character integration — only Andy would say this with zero irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't sneak around, Ann. I'm not sneaky. I'm loud and aggressive and I have a very distinctive walk.

jokes.text: "I want to apologize to all the women and Jerry."
jokes.setup: Chris is formally apologizing for the lewd photo situation affecting the female employees.
jokes.punchline: He tacks on 'and Jerry' — implying Jerry also received the photo, and also implies Jerry is not in the category of 'women' but is still somehow a victim.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical joke. The 'and Jerry' is the entire gag — it implies multiple things simultaneously: that Jerry also received the photo, that Jerry is somehow categorically separate from 'women,' and that Jerry is perpetually unfortunate. Extremely efficient comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ann, look at this email. It has a photo of us from the gala attached.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stop emailing me pictures of yourself! I already have enough photos of you!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I didn't send that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, your photo did. Look at it. Stop it. No more emails!

jokes.text: "If I could go back in time and cut your eyeballs out, I would. / Wow, that is so sweet. Thank you."
jokes.setup: Someone is expressing sympathy to Leslie about having to look at the lewd photo.
jokes.punchline: The 'sympathy' offered is a violent fantasy (going back in time to remove her eyeballs), and Leslie accepts it as a heartfelt compliment.
jokes.explanation: Dark and absurd — the idea of time-traveling eye removal as an act of compassion is genuinely weird and funny. Leslie's sincere gratitude for this violent offer is the perfect reaction. The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of the sympathy gesture and the character comedy of Leslie receiving it warmly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, that's... that's pretty bold. I mean, you gotta admire the audacity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, did I just make a pun? That was accidental.

jokes.text: Leslie's Perd Hapley impression: "Leslie Knope, I'm about to ask you a question right now and that question is this..." followed by the team's delight.
jokes.setup: The team asks Leslie if she can do Perd Hapley, the local news anchor known for his redundant, circular phrasing.
jokes.punchline: Leslie delivers a spot-on impression of Perd's verbal redundancy ('I'm about to ask you a question right now and that question is this') with full commitment.
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley is one of Parks and Rec's great recurring jokes, and Leslie doing his impression is a meta, fan-rewarding moment. The impression captures his specific verbal tic perfectly. High rewatch bonus for fans of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Jerry, if you ever do that again, I'm going to break every bone in your body.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh, Chris, that's the nicest thing anyone's ever said to me.

jokes.text: "Andrew, my mandrew, what you up to? / I'm about to do an experiment where I huck this at the wall and see what happens. But that can wait. Shoe shine?"
jokes.setup: Tom approaches Andy at his shoe-shine stand to offer him a job.
jokes.punchline: Andy is about to throw something at a wall as an 'experiment' — and cheerfully pivots to offer a shoe shine as though these are equivalent activities.
jokes.explanation: A lovely piece of Andy absurdism — calling throwing something at a wall an 'experiment' is perfect for his character, as is the non sequitur pivot to shoe-shining. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Political Advisor 1
dialogue.line: Leslie, we'd like you to do a TV interview.

dialogue.speaker: Political Advisor 2
dialogue.line: We've heard you're great at imitating interviewers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, I do have a talent for that.

dialogue.speaker: Political Advisor 1
dialogue.line: That's perfect! You can anticipate their questions and prepare better answers.

dialogue.speaker: Political Advisor 2
dialogue.line: This is going to be amazing!

jokes.text: I'm just now getting really good at shoe shining. And, I'm still pretty bad at it.
jokes.setup: Tom pitches Andy a job at Entertainment 720, noting his potential
jokes.punchline: Andy's self-assessment simultaneously claims improvement and admits current incompetence — the two halves contradict each other
jokes.explanation: The self-contradiction is perfectly Andy — earnest, lacking self-awareness, and oddly endearing. 'Getting really good' paired with 'still pretty bad' in the same breath is structurally clean and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is my new business card. Pretty cool, right?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Tom, I can't read any of this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's because it's cool. If you can read it, it's not cool enough.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's also on fire.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the destructible element. Very exclusive.

jokes.text: Tom's business card: black print on black background, described as 'the coolest possible color scheme' — also a strong magnet that will destroy your credit cards.
jokes.setup: Tom gives Andy his business card as a recruitment pitch.
jokes.punchline: The card is unreadable (black on black), is actually a strong magnet, and Tom considers these features assets rather than flaws.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Tom Haverford joke. The escalation from 'impossible to read' to 'also a strong magnet' to 'it will destroy your credit cards. Guaranteed.' is beautifully constructed. Tom presenting each flaw as a selling point is peak character comedy, and 'Guaranteed' as a cheerful capper on the credit card destruction is perfectly economical. This joke is comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example — surprising, specific, quotable, and revealing of character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Does it have any destructive properties?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, it's just a regular card.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So it won't help me with my debt?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, Andy, it won't. Now if you'll excuse me, I have to take this call about a penis investigation.

jokes.text: "Destroy my credit cards. Debt and everything?" — Andy processes the magnet card news with apparent excitement.
jokes.setup: Tom has warned Andy that the business card magnet will destroy his credit cards.
jokes.punchline: Andy, rather than being alarmed, seems almost hopeful — asking if it will destroy the debt too.
jokes.explanation: A quick follow-on joke that adds another layer to the business card bit. Andy's financial obliviousness (hoping a magnet might erase his debt) is perfectly in character and gets a solid laugh. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That is disturbing.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Your body is a temple. My body is a finely-tuned instrument of maximum physical potential and performance.

jokes.text: "Mr. Mayor, I promise you that we will find the owner of that wiener, and we will punish him."
jokes.setup: Ben is reporting to the mayor about the lewd photo investigation.
jokes.punchline: The formal official language ('find the owner of that wiener') applied to a penis photo creates an absurd juxtaposition — and 'wiener' is inherently a funny word in a formal context.
jokes.explanation: A solid wordplay joke — the formal bureaucratic register applied to 'wiener' gets a laugh. Functional but relies mostly on the inherent comedy of the word rather than deep craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And that's why we need to invest in our parks. Because let's face it, size matters.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: Well, that's a joke. I recognize the structure of a joke. But I don't understand what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was a penis joke, Perd.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that's inappropriate for television.

jokes.text: "There's something very disturbing about the testicles. / I've always felt the same way myself. The testicles are like the ears of the genital system. They serve a very important function, but they're not that great to look at."
jokes.setup: Someone reports to Chris that there is something disturbing about the testicles in the photo, presumably for medical reasons.
jokes.punchline: Chris goes on a philosophical tangent comparing testicles to ears — they serve a function but aren't aesthetically pleasing.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely original and funny observation. The testicles-as-ears analogy is unexpected, specific, and yet somehow logically defensible in the most absurd way. Chris's serene confidence in delivering this philosophy elevates it. Highly quotable. A strong joke that earns its 8+ score through genuine originality.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: And that's the news. Perd Hapley, news anchor, saying the news. You see, I say 'the news' because I am literally saying news to you right now.

jokes.text: "Ann Perkins. You really know your testes. / Thank you?"
jokes.setup: Ann has just correctly identified a medical condition from a lewd photo.
jokes.punchline: Chris offers this as a sincere, almost admiring compliment. Ann's uncertain 'Thank you?' captures the absurdity perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Chris's earnest compliment and Ann's baffled response is a tight, efficient comedy beat. 'You really know your testes' delivered with total sincerity by Chris is a perfect character moment. The question mark on Ann's 'Thank you?' does a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I got you flowers. They're not just flowers—they're a symbol of my deep affection, combined with the traditional romantic gesture that spans centuries of human courtship, representing both the beauty of nature and the fragility of love itself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, that's... we need to talk.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley (done by Leslie): "Leslie Knope, I'm about to ask you a question right now and that question is this. The lewd photo. Just how big a deal is it? / Well, frankly, Perd, it's not that big a deal, if you know what I mean. / I don't know what you mean, but it had the cadence of a joke."
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing her Perd Hapley impression for the team, with the 'how big a deal is it' question about a lewd photo.
jokes.punchline: Leslie as Perd responds 'it's not that big a deal, if you know what I mean' — a double entendre about penis size. Perd's response ('I don't know what you mean but it had the cadence of a joke') is perfect meta-commentary.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. The layering here is exceptional: (1) Leslie is doing an impression, (2) within the impression she makes a double entendre about the lewd photo, (3) Perd's scripted response acknowledges the joke structure without understanding the content ('it had the cadence of a joke'). The meta-commentary on joke structure IS the punchline. 'It had the cadence of a joke' is a brilliant line that captures Perd Hapley's character perfectly while also being genuinely witty commentary on comedy itself. Very high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It went great! We're now engaged. We're getting married in the spring. And we're having triplets.

jokes.text: "There you have it, where 'it' is the thing Leslie Knope just said about this situation."
jokes.setup: Leslie (as Perd) is wrapping up the interview segment.
jokes.punchline: Perd's signature sign-off involves defining 'it' in his 'There you have it' to mean exactly what was just said — a perfectly circular, content-free statement that is entirely Perd.
jokes.explanation: A strong Perd Hapley joke — the logical tautology of defining 'it' as 'the thing that was just said' is beautifully absurd. It captures Perd's verbal style of saying a lot while communicating nothing. Great character voice work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was going to break up with him, but then he did this thing where he looked at me with those eyes, you know? Those big puppy dog eyes. And I just... I couldn't do it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't just not break up with someone because of their eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Have you SEEN his eyes, Ann?

jokes.text: "That was my brother. He just had a baby girl. / Oh, my God. That's horrible. Or good. Full disclosure, I didn't listen to what you just said."
jokes.setup: Ben shares personal news with Leslie, who is clearly distracted by her own situation.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reaction cycles through horror and recovery before admitting she wasn't listening at all.
jokes.explanation: A good joke about Leslie's distraction. 'That's horrible. Or good.' is a funny mid-correction, and 'Full disclosure, I didn't listen' is a solid confession beat. Well-structured short joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, who sent this? What's the email address?

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: It's... horndog27@swarthmore.edu

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Swarthmore? That's like, one of the best liberal arts colleges in the country.

jokes.text: Ben presents Leslie with an L-shaped éclair. "The 'L' is for Leslie, for your name."
jokes.setup: Ben is about to be broken up with by Leslie.
jokes.punchline: He preempts her by presenting a sweet, absurdly sincere gift — an éclair shaped like her initial — with an explanation of what the L stands for that is both unnecessary and touching.
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny — the L-shaped éclair with the earnest explanation ('for your name') is both a joke about Ben's dorky sincerity and a touching romantic gesture. The comedy comes from his complete guilelessness. Also functions as a callback setup for the next joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Look, sometimes you gotta think of the office like a pipe system. You got your main line—that's me—and everything else is just tributaries flowing into my greatness.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's not how pipes work.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: See, that's what I'm talking about. You're clogged up with negativity. You need to flush that out with some positive P-trap energy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Those are all real plumbing terms and you're using them completely wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Exactly. That's the kind of can-do attitude that gets results.

jokes.text: "Well, I started crying because he gave me an éclair. And then we made out and spent the night together. But this morning, in the cold light of day, I cooked breakfast and we made out some more. / Wow! You opposite of broke up with him. / He gave me an éclair, Ann."
jokes.setup: Ann asks how the breakup went.
jokes.punchline: Leslie describes a series of escalating romantic activities that are the complete opposite of breaking up, culminating in Ann's perfectly coined 'you opposite of broke up with him' — and Leslie's final defensive explanation: 'He gave me an éclair, Ann.'
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke sequence. The escalation ('started crying...made out...spent the night...cooked breakfast...made out some more') builds perfectly to Ann's inspired coinage 'you opposite of broke up with him' — which is both linguistically funny and emotionally accurate. The callback punchline 'He gave me an éclair, Ann' as Leslie's entire defense is perfect: completely inadequate as an explanation, completely understandable as a feeling. One of the episode's top moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So what's the diagnosis?

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Well, the doctor said I have a very rare condition. It's called 'Joe-ing too hard.'

jokes.text: "I've determined that the lewd picture was sent by you, because you sent it from your personal email address, stinkmaster69@alumni.sarahlawrencecollege.edu."
jokes.setup: Ben is formally confronting the employee who sent the lewd photo.
jokes.punchline: The email address is 'stinkmaster69@alumni.sarahlawrencecollege.edu' — the combination of the crude username with the prestigious liberal arts college domain is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on juxtaposition: 'stinkmaster69' is perfectly lowbrow, while Sarah Lawrence College is a prestigious, artsy liberal arts school — the combination is both absurd and very specific in a way that suggests real character. High originality in the specificity of the college choice.

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: High five!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron's afraid of physical contact. He once spent an entire weekend locked in his office because someone sneezed near him.

jokes.text: "Really? Sarah Lawrence? / Yeah. I wanted a small college experience."
jokes.setup: Ben calls out that the employee went to Sarah Lawrence.
jokes.punchline: The employee defends his choice of Sarah Lawrence with the mundane, reasonable explanation 'I wanted a small college experience' — as though that is the relevant issue right now.
jokes.explanation: A strong follow-up to the email address joke. The employee's complete seriousness about his college choice in the middle of a firing is great misdirection — he defends Sarah Lawrence, not the lewd photo. The non sequitur priority is perfectly absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: As the senior staff member present, I'm taking charge of this office.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No one cares.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I love you, Leslie!

jokes.text: "There's an old sewage department saying: 'If you've got a nice drain pipe, there's no reason to hide it.' / I doubt that's a saying."
jokes.setup: The employee is being confronted about sending the lewd photo.
jokes.punchline: He defends himself with a supposed 'old sewage department saying' — an absurd, crude euphemism — and Ben flatly refuses to accept it as a real saying.
jokes.explanation: A solid joke. The 'old sewage department saying' framing gives the lewd logic false gravitas, and Ben's 'I doubt that's a saying' is a perfectly dry straight-man response. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Leslie, I need career advice. Should I stick with my current job or try something new?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, you should absolutely try something new! You need to challenge yourself and grow!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Really? Even though I have a family to support?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you have a family? No, no, no. You need to stay put. Stability is everything. Family comes first.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I thought you said I should challenge myself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, yes, but that was before I knew about the family situation. Although, actually, having a family means you should be even MORE ambitious. Show them what's possible! Pursue your dreams!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So which is it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Both. Neither. Whatever you choose, I will support you 100 percent, but also I will judge you slightly for not picking the other option.

jokes.text: "The law of having an amazing package."
jokes.setup: Ben tells the employee he is being terminated for breaking the law.
jokes.punchline: The employee clarifies which 'law' he believes he violated: 'the law of having an amazing package.'
jokes.explanation: A functional wordplay joke using the double meaning of 'package.' The employee's total lack of shame or self-awareness is consistent and funny. Not deeply original but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Andy, what's troubling you?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I've been thinking about quitting my job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's easy. Just don't think about it. Problem solved.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wow, Leslie, that's actually really helpful advice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. I'm basically a therapist.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're the worst therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you.

jokes.text: "And you have the mumps. You might want to get that checked. / Sweet. Someone's got mumps on his lumps."
jokes.setup: As a final blow, Ben reveals that Ann medically diagnosed the employee with mumps from his lewd photo.
jokes.punchline: The employee's response to learning he has mumps is self-congratulation: 'Sweet. Someone's got mumps on his lumps' — a rhyming, cheerful celebration of his own illness.
jokes.explanation: The rhyme 'mumps on his lumps' is cheerful and rhythmically satisfying, and the employee's unbroken positivity in the face of an STI-adjacent diagnosis is a great character beat. The 'Sweet' opener is a perfect character response.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Treats the parade of genitals like normal email correspondence

jokes.text: "UP high. Anyone? / Ron isn't here."
jokes.setup: The employee goes for a celebratory high-five after being fired and diagnosed with mumps.
jokes.punchline: April delivers a flat, non-sequitur explanation: 'Ron isn't here' — as if Ron would be the only person who might high-five this man, and his absence is the only obstacle.
jokes.explanation: A superb April Ludgate joke. The logic is perfect: she doesn't say 'no' or 'you're fired,' she simply explains that the one person who might have done this isn't here — implying Ron would high-five a man being fired for sending lewd photos, and that everyone else absolutely would not. Near-perfect economy. High character integration for April's specific brand of deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hold on, I'm getting a call. Hello? Oh hey! No, no, we're just in the middle of something really important here. Yeah, okay, I'll call you back. Bye!

dialogue.speaker: Political advisor
dialogue.line: Who was that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My mom.

jokes.text: "You give such good advice. Babe, I love you. / You're welcome."
jokes.setup: April has just given Andy completely useless, contradictory advice that resolved nothing.
jokes.punchline: Andy sincerely thanks her for the 'good advice,' and April accepts the thanks with a straight 'You're welcome' — neither party aware of how bad the advice was.
jokes.explanation: A good button to the advice sequence. The earnestness of both characters' satisfaction with a completely useless exchange is perfectly Andy and April. Slight diminishing return from the previous joke but still lands.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Now it's spread to other cities and departments

jokes.text: "Because now I have everyone in City Hall sending me pictures of their junk, asking me if they have mumps. / Oh, my God. / Your inbox is literally filled with penises."
jokes.setup: Ann tells Leslie that Chris announced her mumps diagnosis — so now every male city employee is sending her genital photos for medical evaluation.
jokes.punchline: "Your inbox is literally filled with penises." — the logical but absurd consequence of the earlier story.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed escalation of the lewd photo subplot. The logic is airtight (men think they might have mumps too) and the image of an inbox 'literally filled with penises' is stated so matter-of-factly that it lands hard. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'll have a glass of your cheapest wine. Actually, you know what? I don't know anything about wine. I don't know if I'm supposed to swirl it or sniff it or what. I just know that it makes me feel warm and loose, and I like how it tastes like fruit sometimes.

jokes.text: "Oh, look. Ed Miller from Payroll." — Leslie looks at Ann's phone and recognizes a sender.
jokes.setup: Ann's phone keeps buzzing with new lewd photos from city employees.
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually identifies a sender by name, implying she recognized the photo — then quickly moves on.
jokes.explanation: A brief but excellent joke. The implication that Leslie recognized 'Ed Miller from Payroll' from his genital photo is left completely unaddressed — perfect deadpan economy. The specificity ('from Payroll') makes it funnier than a generic name would.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need to use the bathroom. Excuse me, where's the pooper?

jokes.text: Oh, look. Ed Miller from Payroll. [Leslie recognizing a new penis photo sender]
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are discussing the cascade of unsolicited photos flooding Ann's inbox
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually recognizes a coworker by their genitalia — the implied familiarity is the horror
jokes.explanation: The casual recognition of a coworker ('Ed Miller from Payroll') by their unsolicited intimate photo is a darkly funny moment. The economy is perfect — one line delivers both the escalation and the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Welcome to my cabin. Here are the ground rules: no talking during meals, no talking during TV time, and no talking while I'm thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? No talking at all. In fact, I'd prefer it if you didn't even breathe too loudly.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And if you must exist in this space, do it as quietly as possible. Ideally, stop existing altogether.

jokes.text: "Do you need to get that? / No, it's just penises."
jokes.setup: Leslie's phone keeps buzzing during a serious conversation about her relationship.
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismisses it with 'No, it's just penises' — the most casual possible response to a phone full of unsolicited genital photos.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — 'No, it's just penises' as a casual dismissal is a great deadpan line. The normalization of this absurd situation is the joke. High quotability for a very short line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what happened with Tammy One?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She violated the rules. I enforced them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What rules? What did she do?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a list. She breathed too loud during dinner. That's a spanking. She used my toothbrush without asking. That's two spankings. She wore the same outfit twice in one week. That's a spanking and no dessert for a month.

jokes.text: "It's the entire Sanitation Department, from Muncie."
jokes.setup: The pattern of city employees sending Ann lewd photos has been established.
jokes.punchline: The escalation reaches an absurd peak: not just one department, but an entire department from a different city — Muncie — has somehow gotten involved.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'from Muncie' is what elevates this above a generic escalation joke. It implies the news has spread beyond Pawnee city limits, which is both absurd and somehow logically consistent with the world of the show. 'From Muncie' is doing enormous comedic work in two words.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm offering you three options: hunting, fishing, or drinking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I choose yoga.

jokes.text: "Would you like any wine to start? / Yes. And I'm going to be direct and honest with you. I would like a glass of red wine, and I'll take the cheapest one you have because I can't tell the difference."
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to have a serious, honest conversation with Ben at a restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Her vow to be 'direct and honest' is immediately applied to the wine order — she admits she can't tell wine apart, so she wants the cheapest.
jokes.explanation: A lovely character joke. Leslie's compulsive directness and honesty, which she's been building up to deploy on Ben, gets hilariously redirected at the waiter first. Her complete lack of wine snobbery is both practical and endearing. Good structure using the 'direct and honest' framing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've arranged for everyone to get comprehensive medical screenings. No more embarrassing photos to share.

dialogue.speaker: Male employee
dialogue.line: That's great, Ben. Thanks for thinking of us.

dialogue.speaker: Male employee
dialogue.line: Hey everyone, check out these X-rays of my spleen!

jokes.text: "I'm going to go to the bathroom. The whiz palace, as we like to call it here."
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to be supportive during the conversation but senses something serious is coming.
jokes.punchline: He excuses himself to the bathroom and refers to it as 'the whiz palace, as we like to call it here' — a cheerful, goofy euphemism delivered in a tense moment.
jokes.explanation: Ben's nervous energy manifesting as a goofy euphemism ('the whiz palace') is a nice character beat. The 'as we like to call it here' — spoken in a restaurant where he presumably doesn't work — adds absurdist texture. Solid and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've been reading about Richard Branson. That guy's a total inspiration. He started Virgin Records in his parents' basement.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was born in my parents' basement.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My parents didn't believe in hospitals. They thought they were a conspiracy by the government to make us dependent on the state. So my mom just squatted over a bucket for six hours while my dad read to her from a pamphlet about natural childbirth that he printed off the internet on our dial-up connection.

jokes.text: Ron appears at Leslie's bathroom window while she is having her restaurant conversation with Ben.
jokes.setup: Leslie has gone to the restaurant bathroom to compose herself during the difficult conversation with Ben.
jokes.punchline: Ron, who is supposedly hiding from Tammy One, has tracked Leslie down and is at her bathroom window — fleeing his own problems by running to Leslie's.
jokes.explanation: Ron appearing at a bathroom window while ostensibly hiding is a strong visual gag. The irony of the man who just fled the office now showing up at someone's bathroom window is rich. High character integration — Ron would absolutely do this.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't want to work for a logo company.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, that's exactly what we might become.

jokes.text: Ron's three rules for staying at his cabin: "One, no talk about Tammy One. Two, no talk about Ben. Three, no talk."
jokes.setup: Ron is reluctantly allowing Leslie to stay with him while they both avoid their problems.
jokes.punchline: His rules escalate from specific prohibitions (Tammy One, Ben) to a total prohibition on all talking — the final rule swallowing the first two.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional joke. The structure is perfect: two specific rules that seem reasonable for Ron, then the third rule reveals that he actually just doesn't want ANY talking — the specificity of rules 1 and 2 was a red herring. The escalation to 'no talk' as the ultimate rule is the cleanest possible punchline and is completely true to Ron's character. Extremely quotable. One of the episode's best moments and comparable to the 8.0 calibration anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've prepared for every possible wilderness survival scenario. Hypothermia, bear attacks, flash floods, getting lost for days without food or water.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's... actually impressive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you! I have freeze-dried meals, a water purification system, emergency flares, a first aid kit, and seventeen different s'mores recipes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: ...Did you say seventeen s'mores recipes?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: For any campfire dessert emergency. Classic, chocolate chip, peppermint bark, salted caramel—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're prepared for dessert emergencies.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You never know when you'll need s'mores.

jokes.text: "I didn't even ask you last night. What is going on with Tammy One? / You just violated rules number one and three. You lose your coffee privileges."
jokes.setup: Leslie immediately breaks Ron's rules by asking about Tammy One.
jokes.punchline: Ron enforces the rules immediately and with great specificity — not just 'you broke the rules' but naming which rules (one AND three) and assigning a specific punishment (coffee privileges).
jokes.explanation: A strong callback that pays off the three-rules joke immediately. The precision of 'rules number one and three' — and the fact that coffee is the punishment currency — is perfect Ron Swanson logic. The idea of 'coffee privileges' as a cabin disciplinary mechanism is both absurd and completely believable for Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When I was eight, I fell off a horse and broke my arm in two places. My parents took me to the emergency room, and on the way home, we stopped for ice cream. My dad said, 'Well, Leslie, you've learned an important lesson today.' I said, 'What's that, Dad?' He said, 'Never break your arm in just one place.'

jokes.text: "You choose, Knope. Hunting, fishing or drinking? / I'd really love to shoot a gun right now. / Fishing it is."
jokes.setup: Ron offers Leslie a choice of activities at the cabin.
jokes.punchline: Leslie chooses 'shoot a gun' (hunting) — but Ron overrides her choice and picks fishing, as if he was going to choose fishing regardless of what she said.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection here is clean and economical: the 'choice' is revealed to not be a real choice at all. Ron's override of Leslie's preference as though it doesn't register is perfect Ron Swanson autonomy. Also adds a small character detail that Leslie wanted to shoot a gun to process her feelings — very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, why do you only have nine toes?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't want to talk about it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, tell me what happened.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A man is entitled to his mysteries.

jokes.text: Councilman (or official) asks: "What if based on empirical evidence, I truly believe there is a grave and immediate medical emergency? Were that the case, could I then show you my dong?"
jokes.setup: Chris has just announced that male employees must stop sending Ann explicit photos.
jokes.punchline: An official raises a procedural 'what if' exception — framing the lewd photo as a 'grave and immediate medical emergency' covered by empirical evidence.
jokes.explanation: The bureaucratic framing of an inappropriate request — treating it like a procedural exception with 'empirical evidence' and 'grave and immediate medical emergency' — is very funny. The formal language makes the crude punchline ('could I then show you my dong') land hard.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, that was insensitive. I apologize.

jokes.text: "Now, completely different scenario. Let's say, I've been watching a lot of women's golf and I've had some wine."
jokes.setup: The official's first exception was rejected (joke #47); he immediately offers another scenario.
jokes.punchline: The 'completely different scenario' is even less defensible than the first: watching women's golf and drinking wine as justification.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'medical emergency' to 'women's golf and wine' is perfect — the second scenario is somehow both more specific and more ridiculous than the first. The specificity of 'women's golf' as the arousal catalyst is genuinely surprising and funny. One of the better jokes in the subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, I've had a lot of jobs in my life. I've been a shoe shiner, a shoe repair guy, a shoe... loser. But you know what? Every single one of those jobs was an incredible adventure. I mean, who else can say they've spent eight hours organizing alphabetically by heel height? That's not work, that's a calling.

jokes.text: "Perfect. Just as a backup, I'm sending you some photos. / That will not be necessary. / That's me."
jokes.setup: Chris has offered to bring in a male doctor to do screenings instead.
jokes.punchline: The official has apparently already sent photos — and identifies them as himself before Ann can even respond to the idea.
jokes.explanation: A good button to the sequence. 'That's me' — delivered as though identifying himself in a photo is perfectly ordinary — is a funny and economical final beat for this subplot. The rapid-fire timing works well.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'll help you find a new career. You could be a shoe-shinist.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A what?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: A shoe-shinist. Someone who shines shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I think it's 'shoe shiner.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, shoe-shinist. It sounds more professional.

jokes.text: Tom distributes Entertainment 720 branded merchandise to the Parks Department: umbrella, flyswatters, Rubik's Cube with his face on it, breath mints, fireplace bellows, and a drum roll sound effect keychain.
jokes.setup: Tom is back at the Parks Department, ostensibly for 'high-level networking.'
jokes.punchline: The branded merchandise escalates in absurdity: umbrella (plausible) → flyswatters (odd) → Rubik's Cube with his face on it (bizarre) → fireplace bellows (completely inexplicable) → drum roll sound effect keychain.
jokes.explanation: An escalating absurdist list joke. The merchandise escalates perfectly: each item is more inexplicable than the last, with 'fireplace bellows' being the peak of absurdity (who orders branded fireplace bellows?) and the drum roll keychain serving as a meta-joke (he makes his own drum roll for the reveal). High originality and character integration — this list exists in Tom Haverford's specific universe.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I really want to kiss you right now.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Then why don't you?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because I'm at work and I have a customer.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey buddy, I'm gonna have to redo all of this work. Sorry about that.

jokes.text: "You think Bethenny Frankel sits behind a desk all day? She makes $100 million a year. How much do you make a year? / $101 million."
jokes.setup: April challenges Tom on whether he's actually working by being at the Parks Department.
jokes.punchline: Tom responds to April's implied financial critique by claiming he makes $101 million a year — one more than Bethenny Frankel.
jokes.explanation: The '$101 million' is a perfect joke — it's not that he claims an obscene amount, it's that he specifies exactly one million more than Bethenny Frankel, suggesting he's keenly tracking her income. It's both absurd and deeply revealing of Tom's competitive, celebrity-obsessed personality. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm running for City Council!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You need to sign an anti-tax pledge. Immediately.

jokes.text: "I, for one, am happy to see Tom. / Thanks, Jerry. Here. Have an umbrella and some breath strips."
jokes.setup: Everyone is dismissive of Tom; Jerry is the only one who welcomes him.
jokes.punchline: Tom thanks Jerry — the lowest-status person in the office — and gives him the least impressive gifts as a reward for loyalty.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat. The running gag of Jerry being the one who enthusiastically supports the wrong things is here. Tom's reflexive 'Thanks, Jerry' with the consolation prize gifts is a good double beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'll do it for free!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, Andy, you need to be paid.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Are you kidding? I get to work with you? I would pay you.

jokes.text: Jerry's reaction — possibly excited — upon receiving an umbrella and breath strips, implying he considers this a good outcome.
jokes.setup: Jerry has expressed support for Tom and receives the least impressive branded merchandise.
jokes.punchline: The 'Whoa!' reaction suggests Jerry is genuinely pleased or surprised by these ordinary items — his perpetual enthusiasm for small things is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat for Jerry but not a strongly constructed joke. His reaction is inferrable but not given much material to work with.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy One will find me. She's like a hunting dog, except instead of tracking birds, she tracks men who are trying to escape her.

jokes.text: "All right, enough chit-chat, everyone. Please get back to work. / You're not our boss. / What did you just say to me? / Ma'am."
jokes.setup: April, as acting manager, tries to assert authority over Tom.
jokes.punchline: Tom initially challenges her ('What did you just say to me?') as though he's in charge, then immediately backs down and calls her 'Ma'am' — a complete capitulation.
jokes.explanation: Tom's bluster followed by instant capitulation ('Ma'am') is well-structured. The joke is the gap between his posturing and his actual deference to April. Good character work for both.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: The doctor said I'm perfectly healthy, but he was distracted during the exam because he kept staring at my... well, he didn't finish the full examination. But that's fine, I'm sure everything is fine.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Although, come to think of it, he did say he'd call me back because he forgot to check... actually, you know what, I bet he just wanted an excuse to call me.

jokes.text: "I think it'd be kind of cool to work for Tom. / So, take it. / But, working at a start-up can be kind of risky. / So, don't take it. / But Tom told me to follow my dreams. / So, take it. / But this isn't my dream. / So, don't take it. / I don't know what to do. / Me, neither."
jokes.setup: The same advice exchange as before, now with Tom present and slightly different content.
jokes.punchline: The exact same structure plays out again, confirming April's advice methodology.
jokes.explanation: A diminishing return on the advice joke from earlier. The structure is the same and the episode has already done this. Functions more as a running gag beat than a standalone joke. Still gets a laugh but the first version was stronger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I have to break up with you. And I'm going to be really mean about it to make it easier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're... you're stupid!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, wait. You smell like a... like a foot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A dirty foot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not even—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And your face looks like... like a regular face. But bad.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And I hope you step on a Lego. A really sharp one.

jokes.text: I think there might be a place for you over at Entertainment 720. What is that? My Company. Oh, I don't know, Tom. I'm just now getting really good at shoe shining. And, I'm still pretty bad at it.
jokes.setup: Tom is making his final pitch to Andy for the job.
jokes.punchline: Andy's hesitation is that he's getting 'really good' at shoe shining — undercut immediately by admitting he's still bad at it. (Second iteration of the Joke 22 sentiment, applied to a new conversation.)
jokes.explanation: A callback to the earlier shoe-shining joke but with diminishing returns since it's essentially the same beat. Works as character reinforcement but scores lower than the original because the originality is gone.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I knew something was off when you said you were at the dentist, but your teeth looked exactly the same.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I have naturally white teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you also said the dentist gave you a lollipop, but you had lipstick on your teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was a red lollipop!

jokes.text: "I figure we build a fire, roast the fish we shot, and make s'mores. / I don't have the material for s'mores. / I do. I always carry emergency s'more rations in my car."
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron are at the cabin by a lake, planning their activities.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has 'emergency s'more rations' in her car at all times — she is perpetually prepared for spontaneous s'mores, which is both absurd and completely consistent with her hyper-organized, optimistic character.
jokes.explanation: A lovely Leslie joke. 'Emergency s'more rations' as a concept — implying there are non-emergency s'more situations that require pre-stocked supplies — is both absurd and perfectly Leslie. The casual 'I always carry' suggests this is simply a feature of her life. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I realized these weren't Leslie's normal sleep speeches. Her normal ones are about zoning regulations and park maintenance. These were actual campaign speeches with policy positions and everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So I knew something was up. Leslie was awake. She was actually running for office.

jokes.text: I don't have the material for s'mores. / I do. I always carry emergency s'more rations in my car.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests s'mores; Ron says he doesn't have the materials
jokes.punchline: Leslie has 'emergency s'more rations' in her car — the preparedness is funny, as is the idea that s'mores constitute an emergency supply category
jokes.explanation: 'Emergency s'more rations' is the joke — Leslie having a dedicated emergency category for s'mores in her car is absurdly specific and very Leslie. The deadpan delivery ('I always carry') makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: I'm here to help you, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Help me with what?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: Well, back when we were married, I tried to kill you. Twice. But I'm over that now.

jokes.text: "Given your hunting abilities and my chocolate supply, I figure we could stay up here for two, three years?"
jokes.setup: Leslie has emergency s'mores and Ron has fishing skills.
jokes.punchline: Leslie leaps to a two-to-three year timeline for hiding in the woods based on these supplies — suggesting she is seriously considering never dealing with her problems.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'two, three years' as a reasonable survivalist estimate based on fish and s'mores is a funny escalation. Leslie's planning instincts applied to avoidance is a rich character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy One
dialogue.line: Your posture is atrocious. You sit like a question mark.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for that feedback, Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your posture is fine. You sit like an exclamation point!

jokes.text: Ron's story: his brother shot him in the pinky toe with a nail gun as a "hilarious prank" and they "all had a good laugh," he avoided the doctor, and the toe "just kind of fell off." He now has nine toes.
jokes.setup: Ron is about to make a point about avoiding problems (a metaphor for Leslie's situation with Ben).
jokes.punchline: The anecdote he uses is that his brother shot him with a nail gun, he refused to see a doctor because of paperwork, and his toe fell off — and the moral he draws is still "you can't run away from your problems."
jokes.explanation: An outstanding Ron Swanson joke sequence. Every element is perfectly calibrated: the nail gun presented as a 'hilarious prank,' the avoidance of the doctor due to paperwork hate (not pain — paperwork), the toe simply 'falling off' as a casual detail, and the moral lesson STILL being about not running from problems despite this story being about exactly that. The reveal that Ron has nine toes is a perfect final beat. One of the episode's top moments in terms of character specificity and structural comedy.

jokes.text: "You can't run away from your problems. Especially if you only have nine toes. / Sorry. That was uncalled for."
jokes.setup: Leslie is receiving Ron's wisdom about not running away from problems.
jokes.punchline: She can't resist making a joke about the nine toes, then immediately apologizes — she knows she crossed a line but couldn't help herself.
jokes.explanation: A superb callback and a perfectly Leslie reaction. The 'especially if you only have nine toes' punchline is excellent — unexpected but earned — and Leslie's immediate self-correction ('Sorry. That was uncalled for.') adds a second layer of character comedy. The apology makes it funnier. Strong structure and character integration.

jokes.text: You can't run away from your problems. Especially if you only have nine toes. / Sorry. That was uncalled for.
jokes.setup: Leslie turns Ron's story into life advice about not running away from problems
jokes.punchline: Leslie adds '...especially if you only have nine toes' and then immediately apologizes — the joke works because she knows it was mean but couldn't resist
jokes.explanation: The callback to the nine toes works excellently because it's Leslie weaponizing the information she just got in a gentle roast, then immediately feeling guilty. The self-correction ('sorry, that was uncalled for') makes it funnier because she clearly doesn't regret it.

jokes.text: "I'm Ron Swanson, and you're Leslie...Knope."
jokes.setup: Ron is giving Leslie a motivational speech to stop avoiding her situation.
jokes.punchline: His entire motivational technique is stating their names — as if identity itself is the reminder she needs. The pause before 'Knope' (inferrable from the ellipsis) adds weight to her last name, implying 'you're Leslie, you DON'T say no, you're a Knope who KNOWS what to do.'
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical and emotionally resonant joke. Ron's entire pep talk is two people's names, delivered with complete seriousness. It works as comedy (the inadequacy of 'here are our names' as motivation) and as genuine character warmth simultaneously. The implied wordplay on 'Knope/know' is subtle and the pause makes it land. Very quotable as a standalone Ron Swansonism.

jokes.text: "What is your dream? / It's to be the biggest rock star on the planet, obviously. But that could take another three to five years."
jokes.setup: Tom asks Andy what his dream is, as a motivational pitch.
jokes.punchline: Andy's dream is global rock stardom — which he states as though it's a given that he will achieve it, just on a three-to-five-year timeline.
jokes.explanation: A very strong Andy Dwyer joke. The 'obviously' — as though global rock stardom is the self-evident answer to what anyone's dream would be — and the '3-5 year' business-plan timeline for becoming the biggest rock star on the planet are both perfectly Andy. High character integration.

jokes.text: "One year from now, you, Andy Dwyer, will no longer be a shoe-shinist."
jokes.setup: April is motivating Andy to pursue something more fulfilling.
jokes.punchline: April's inspirational declaration uses the word 'shoe-shinist' — a completely made-up but logical portmanteau for Andy's job title, delivered with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: The invented word 'shoe-shinist' delivered earnestly in an inspirational context is a neat piece of wordplay. April's deadpan commitment to this incorrect but logical title is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: "Kyle, beat it. I'm going to make out with my wife now. / But you've only done half of one of my shoes. / Here. / Now, I haven't done anything. Scram, kid."
jokes.setup: Andy is inspired by April's speech and decides to immediately leave his post to make out with his wife.
jokes.punchline: He dismisses his current customer mid-shoe-shine, gives him his shoe back, and then tells him to leave — and Kyle has now received zero work on his shoe.
jokes.explanation: A strong character beat. The escalating customer abandonment — from 'half a shoe' to 'here, have your shoe back, now I've done nothing, leave' — is a well-structured escalation. Andy's complete guilelessness about abandoning his customer is perfectly Andy.

jokes.text: "Will you pledge right now not to raise taxes? / I think that's premature. / No pledge, no vote."
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she is running for City Council.
jokes.punchline: Jerry immediately pivots to demanding a no-tax-raise pledge before she can even finish — and threatens to withhold his vote, as though that's a meaningful lever.
jokes.explanation: A functional political joke that also characterizes Jerry as a one-issue voter who thinks his vote carries leverage over his direct superior. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Will you pledge right now not to raise taxes? / I think that's premature. / No pledge, no vote.
jokes.setup: The department learns Leslie is running for office and someone asks for a commitment
jokes.punchline: Jerry immediately attempts to extract a no-tax-raise pledge — and when Leslie declines to commit, responds with 'no pledge, no vote' — a voter cliché from the most meek person in the room
jokes.explanation: Jerry deploying hardball voter negotiation tactics on Leslie is funny given his usual meekness. 'No pledge, no vote' from Jerry is an unexpected move. Solid character comedy.

jokes.text: "Leslie, I'm going to work my ass off for you. I'll do anything you ask me. I will prove myself. You don't even have to pay me. / No. Honey. No. I will... / Tomorrow, there will be a 300-page orientation booklet, as well as a dozen homemade cookies in the shape of your face."
jokes.setup: Andy has just been assigned as Leslie's assistant and is expressing his enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response to Andy's heartfelt pledge is to promise a 300-page orientation booklet AND cookies shaped like his face — which is both absurdly excessive and completely Leslie.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful Leslie joke. 300 pages for an assistant orientation booklet is already absurd; adding homemade face-shaped cookies reveals the full Leslie Knope welcome package. The escalation from bureaucratic excess to personal warmth in two sentences is perfectly Leslie. High character integration.

jokes.text: Leslie, I'm going to work my ass off for you. I'll do anything you ask me. I will prove myself. You don't even have to pay me. No. Honey. No.
jokes.setup: Andy has just been spontaneously appointed Leslie's assistant.
jokes.punchline: Andy's enthusiastic pledge includes 'you don't even have to pay me' — and April's alarmed 'No. Honey. No.' is the reaction of someone who knows Andy actually means it and is trying to prevent their household from losing income.
jokes.explanation: April's 'No. Honey. No.' — escalating alarm at Andy's offer to work for free — is the joke. She's not touched by his enthusiasm; she's horrified by the financial implications. This is a very specific married-couple dynamic expressed in three words. The character integration is excellent: only this couple would have this specific problem.

jokes.text: Tomorrow, there will be a 300-page orientation booklet, as well as a dozen homemade cookies in the shape of your face.
jokes.setup: Leslie accepts Andy as her assistant and welcomes him
jokes.punchline: Leslie's welcome package includes a 300-page orientation document AND cookies shaped like Andy's face — both extremes of Leslie's character in one sentence
jokes.explanation: The pairing of 300-page document (Leslie the overachiever) with face-shaped cookies (Leslie the nurturer) is perfectly Leslie. The absurdity of making cookies in the shape of someone's face as a professional gesture is funny and endearing.

jokes.text: "If any of you need anything at all, too bad. Deal with your problems yourselves, like adults. I'll be in my office, waiting for Tammy One."
jokes.setup: Ron returns to work after his cabin retreat and reasserts authority.
jokes.punchline: His management philosophy is explicit dismissal ('too bad'), followed by the admission that he is waiting in his office for his terrifying ex-wife rather than working.
jokes.explanation: A strong Ron return moment. 'Too bad. Deal with your problems yourselves, like adults.' as a management announcement is quintessential Ron, and undercutting it immediately with 'I'll be in my office waiting for Tammy One' — not working, WAITING for his tormentor — is a great structural joke. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: There's no need. She'll find me. She has the tracking ability and body odor of a bloodhound.
jokes.setup: Someone offers to find Tammy One for Ron
jokes.punchline: Ron's description of his ex-wife — 'tracking ability and body odor of a bloodhound' — is horrifying but delivered as a matter-of-fact character assessment
jokes.explanation: The bloodhound comparison is simultaneously insulting and admiring — Ron respects her abilities even while fearing her. The pairing of 'tracking ability' (competence) with 'body odor' (the actual animal quality) is the specific detail that makes it excellent.

jokes.text: "There's no need. She'll find me. She has the tracking ability and body odor of a bloodhound."
jokes.setup: Leslie offers to find Tammy One for Ron.
jokes.punchline: Ron declines, noting that Tammy One will track him herself — because she has the abilities and smell of a bloodhound.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional characterization joke. Tammy One is described with complete deadpan seriousness as having 'the tracking ability and body odor of a bloodhound' — which is both an insult and an acknowledgment of her terrifying capabilities. Ron's tone implies genuine respect for her predatory skills. Very quotable and perfectly Ron.

jokes.text: "That man has the largest penis I have ever seen. I actually don't even know if he has mumps. I forgot to look. I was distracted, by the largest penis I have ever seen."
jokes.setup: The male doctor has done screenings of city employees as promised. Ann reports on the results.
jokes.punchline: Ann's medical report is entirely about one man's anatomy, which she has apparently been unable to process professionally. She repeats the key observation twice, the second time explaining the repetition.
jokes.explanation: A strong joke with good structure. The callback to the mumps diagnosis is immediately subverted — she forgot to even check. The repeated statement ('the largest penis I have ever seen') with the self-explanation ('I was distracted, by the largest penis I have ever seen') creates a circular, funny confession. Ann's professional composure completely collapsed is good character comedy.

jokes.text: Ben pre-emptively breaking up with himself for Leslie: "It's not you, it's me. I'm not ready for a commitment. I just don't like you anymore. I know it's hard to hear that, but — You're boring. And, frankly, you disgust me."
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to break up with Ben but he keeps interrupting her with gifts and knowledge that he already knows about her campaign. He offers to 'make it easy' for her.
jokes.punchline: Ben's version of 'making it easy' is delivering a series of increasingly brutal break-up clichés and genuine insults — ending with 'You're boring. And frankly, you disgust me' — all said in a helpful, generous tone to spare her the work.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is excellent: Ben frames his impersonation of a bad break-up as an act of generosity, then the clichés escalate ('not ready for commitment' → 'don't like you anymore' → 'you're boring' → 'you disgust me'). The escalation from break-up cliché to genuine-sounding insult is perfectly calibrated. Ben delivering 'you disgust me' in a helpful tone is outstanding character work. Leslie's 'Ugh!' reaction is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Okay. Then, I'll just open the box for you. / Please stop bringing out the box.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to break up with Ben; Ben keeps producing a box (likely a ring or gift)
jokes.punchline: Ben offers to open the box to ease the conversation; Leslie's 'please stop bringing out the box' reveals her terror at whatever it contains and the impossibility of breaking up under these conditions
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy structurally — the box keeps appearing as a weapon against Leslie's resolve. 'Please stop bringing out the box' captures Leslie's desperation at having her breakup repeatedly sabotaged by Ben's sweetness.

jokes.text: It's not you, it's me. I'm not ready for a commitment. I just don't like you anymore. I know it's hard to hear that, but... You're boring. And, frankly, you disgust me.
jokes.setup: Ben offers to make the breakup easier for Leslie by saying the lines himself
jokes.punchline: Ben's self-deprecating lines escalate from clichéd ('it's not you, it's me') to increasingly harsh insults about himself ('you disgust me'), voluntarily destroying his own image to protect Leslie's campaign
jokes.explanation: Excellent sequence. The escalation from standard breakup clichés to 'you disgust me' is perfectly structured — each line worse than the last, all delivered by Ben about himself. The structural escalation is textbook and the character motivation (protecting Leslie) gives it emotional weight that makes it funnier.

jokes.text: "How did you figure it out? / Leslie, there was a dude in the ladies' yacht club. / Yeah, but I covered that pretty well."
jokes.setup: Leslie is surprised Ben figured out she was running for office.
jokes.punchline: Ben points to the obvious tell — a man in the ladies' yacht club — and Leslie defends her cover story, suggesting she thought 'Anchors away, ladies' was convincing.
jokes.explanation: A strong callback to the yacht club cover story. Leslie's earnest belief that 'Anchors away, ladies' was adequate camouflage for Ben being in a women's club is perfectly Leslie. Ben's understatement ('there was a dude') is a good straight-man line.

jokes.text: "Also, you've been making campaign speeches in your sleep. Granted, you always do that, but they got really specific and moving."
jokes.setup: Ben explains how he knew Leslie was running for office.
jokes.punchline: He reveals that Leslie makes campaign speeches in her sleep — which he notes she ALWAYS does — but recently they got suspiciously specific.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The revelation that Leslie always makes campaign speeches in her sleep is already perfect character comedy — but the modifier 'Granted, you always do that' is what makes this exceptional. Ben has simply accepted this as a normal part of dating Leslie. The capper 'but they got really specific and moving' adds a beautiful note of genuine admiration within the absurdity. This joke only works for Leslie Knope and Ben Wyatt — near-perfect character integration. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: "Did I have a good opening line? / It was simple, but I liked it."
jokes.setup: Leslie has been making campaign speeches in her sleep.
jokes.punchline: Her first question is about the quality of her opening line — she is immediately treating her unconscious speech-making as a creative product to critique.
jokes.explanation: A strong follow-up beat. Leslie's complete comfort with the fact that she speechifies in her sleep — and her immediate pivot to quality control ('did I have a good opening line?') — is perfectly Leslie. Ben's warm answer ('It was simple, but I liked it') transitions beautifully into the speech itself.

jokes.text: Tammy One arrives. Ron: "Hello, Tammy." Tammy: "Ronald." Ron: "That's enough small talk."
jokes.setup: Ron's terrifying ex-wife Tammy One has finally appeared.
jokes.punchline: The exchange of first names constitutes 'enough small talk' for Ron — he treats two words as excessive pleasantry.
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical and perfectly Ron. Two first names exchanged = 'enough small talk' is a joke about Ron's hatred of social pleasantry, and in this context also about the charged, dangerous nature of this particular relationship. Near-perfect economy. Very quotable as a Ron Swansonism.

jokes.text: "Yes. You ruin people's lives."
jokes.setup: Tammy One reminds Ron that she remembers what she does for a living.
jokes.punchline: Ron confirms her occupation is 'ruining people's lives' — stated as flatly as if she were an accountant.
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical joke. The deadpan delivery of 'You ruin people's lives' as a professional description, with zero emotional escalation, is Ron Swanson at his best. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: "Call it nostalgia. Or, perhaps, guilt for all the times I tried to smother you in your sleep."
jokes.setup: Tammy One claims she is there as a friend.
jokes.punchline: She attributes her motivations to 'guilt' — specifically guilt for repeatedly attempting to smother Ron in his sleep, presented as a slightly embarrassing past habit.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional dark joke. The phrasing 'all the times I tried to smother you in your sleep' — plural, matter-of-fact, offered as a casually mentioned past behavior rather than a shocking confession — is brilliantly written. It establishes Tammy One's character instantly and completely. The word 'all' (implying multiple attempts) does enormous work. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: "Sit up straight. You're not doing your breasts any favors. / Thank you. / Honey, your breasts look amazing."
jokes.setup: Tammy One delivers what appears to be a cutting remark to Leslie about her posture.
jokes.punchline: Leslie takes 'you're not doing your breasts any favors' as a genuine posture tip and thanks her. Then the episode ends with someone (likely Ben or Ann) reassuring Leslie that her breasts look amazing — a warm, absurd button.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful ending joke. Tammy One's backhanded insult is accepted as sincere advice by Leslie (who says 'Thank you') — and then the episode ends with a warm, sincere reassurance about the breasts in question. The tripart exchange (insult → grateful receipt → reassurance) is a perfect comedic button for the episode. Leslie's earnest 'Thank you' for what is clearly an insult is peak Leslie.

tmdb_overview: Leslie is torn between Ben and her dreams of running for public office, while Ron braces himself for the arrival of his first wife, the original Tammy.
insight: Season premiere establishes Leslie's ambition with 61 jokes in 24 minutes—highest density opener of the run.
